how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Pet grooming bid calculator

How much should I charge for dog grooming?

A flat "$X per dog" price prices the breed, not the job. A 12-lb short-coat dog and a 90-lb doodle with a matted double coat are not the same amount of work, and neither is a routine bath-and-brush compared to one that needs a de-shedding treatment, a nail grind, and careful work through mats. Every one of those differences is billed time or billed materials, and it doesn't show up unless you put it in the quote.

Open the free pet grooming bid calculator

What a flat "per dog" price cannot see

Size and coat. A giant, curly-coated dog can take close to twice the hands-on time of a small, short-coated one — bathing, drying, brushing out, and scissoring all scale with size and coat texture.

Matting. A few small mats add a little time. A coat matted to the skin adds a lot of time — and it is also a welfare and safety question a groomer or vet has to make, not just a pricing one. This tool prices the extra time; it never decides whether the groom should happen.

Add-ons. Nail trims, nail grinding, teeth brushing, ear cleaning, de-shedding, flea/tick treatment, and anal gland expression each have their own time and, for some, their own material cost. Priced separately, a customer only pays for what their pet actually needs.

A bid you can defend

  1. Start from a base time for the dog's size, then adjust for coat type.
  2. Add time and a surcharge for matting severity — and stop to check the skin and the animal's temperament before pricing anything past "light".
  3. Add the time and price of every add-on the customer wants.
  4. Add travel time and mileage if you groom on-site, plus supplies, overhead, and a payment fee.
  5. Solve for the price that leaves your target margin after all of it.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. It's not a promise of profit, an animal-health assessment, or a recommendation to accept a job — it's arithmetic on the numbers you enter, for you to check against your own rates and your own judgment about the animal in front of you.

Worked example

A medium dog with a medium coat and no matting is about a 69-minute groom at the calculator's defaults. Add light matting (15 more minutes), a nail trim and ear cleaning (20 more minutes, $27 in add-on pricing), and the job grows past an hour before travel is even in the picture. A $75 quote that looked fine for a basic bath-and-brush can be thin once the real job — mats and add-ons included — is priced in full.

Common questions

How much should I charge for dog grooming?

Start from size and coat, not a flat breed price: a small short-coat dog might be a 45-minute groom, while a giant doodle with a curly coat can take nearly twice as long before you even account for matting or add-ons. Multiply the base time by a loaded hourly rate, add any matting surcharge and add-on time and price, add supplies and overhead, and add travel if you groom on-site.

Why does matting change the price so much?

A few small mats add maybe 15 minutes; a coat matted to the skin can add an hour or more of careful, slow work, and it is also a welfare and safety question, not just a time question — matting that reaches the skin can hide sores or skin damage that changes whether the groom should happen at all. Price the extra time, and treat severe matting as a judgment call for you or a vet, not a box to check for a bigger invoice.

Should add-ons like nail trims and de-shedding be priced separately?

Yes. Each add-on has its own time and, often, its own material cost — a nail trim is a few minutes, a de-shedding treatment can add twenty minutes and its own shampoo cost. Bundling them into one flat groom price either overcharges the customer who wants a basic bath and cut or undercharges the one who wants everything.

Common questions

Does this calculator decide whether an animal is safe or healthy enough to groom?

No. This tool only does arithmetic on the time and cost of a groom you have already decided to do. It does not assess animal welfare, temperament, or health, and it never will. A severely matted coat can hide skin damage, sores, or irritation that needs a veterinarian or vet tech rather than a bigger invoice, and a fearful or aggressive animal is a safety call for the groomer, not a pricing input. If you are not confident an animal is fit and safe to groom, refer it out — do not use this calculator to price around that judgment call.

Why does severe matting require checking a box before it prices?

Matting that reaches the skin can hide cuts, pressure sores, or skin infection underneath, and shaving it out can worsen an injury that was not visible from the surface. The calculator will not turn a severe-matting selection into a quote until you confirm you have actually checked the skin and judged the animal safe to groom — the same way it will not print a negative price when fees and margin exceed 100%. This is not a substitute for that judgment; it only refuses to let the judgment be skipped silently.

How is the base groom time calculated from size and coat?

Each weight tier has a base number of minutes for bathing, drying, and grooming — 45 for a small dog under 25 lb up to 105 for a giant dog over 90 lb — multiplied by a coat factor: 1.0 for short/smooth coats, 1.15 for medium, 1.35 for long or double coats, and 1.6 for curly or doodle coats that need real brush-out and scissor time. Matting minutes and any add-on minutes are added on top of that base.

What happens if the payment fee and target margin together claim the whole price?

The page flags it instead of printing a number. If fee percent plus margin percent reaches or passes 100%, no price can satisfy both claims at once — the tool shows this as unreachable rather than a negative or infinite "quote," which would read as real advice.

Is my pricing or customer information uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculation and the proposal both run in your browser; your saved business details and any usage counts stay in local storage on this device, never sent to a server, and the opt-out checkbox above turns usage counting off entirely.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your business details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, veterinary, or animal-health determination — those depend on your own judgment and a veterinarian's, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

vs-a-flat-per-breed-price.html.text:
← Pet grooming bid calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-breed price card

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic method every groomer already has: a price card by size — small, medium, large, giant — quoted the same regardless of coat, matting, or add-ons.

First — the price card is right, and you should have one

A website, a phone quote, or a sheet on the wall needs one number per size before the dog is in front of you. "Medium dogs $75" is a fine headline price, and no calculator replaces having one. What follows is not an argument that the card is wrong. It is what the same flat number stops showing you the moment the dog is on the table and you can see the coat.

The worked example

Both rows below quote the identical $75 medium-dog card price from this calculator's own starting numbers. The only thing that changes between them is the coat, the matting, and three common add-ons — nail trim, ear cleaning, and de-shedding.

QuestionSimple — medium coat, no matting, no add-onsReal — curly coat, moderate matting, 3 add-ons
What the price card shows $75 — medium dog $75 — medium dog, unchanged
Groom time 69 minutes 171 minutes — nearly 3× as long, and the card cannot see coat or matting
Matting surcharge $0 — no matting $30.00 — moderate matting across the coat
Add-on charges $0 — none selected $52.00 — nail trim, ear cleaning, de-shedding
Direct costs this job actually carries $11.00 (supplies + overhead) $93.00 (supplies + overhead + matting surcharge + add-ons)
Break-even price $11.34 — far below the $75 card price $95.88 — already above the $75 card price, before any profit
What $75 actually nets after costs and the fee $61.75 — an 82.3% margin −$20.25 — a real loss, a −27.0% margin
Effective hourly $53.70 an hour −$7.11 an hour — paying to do the job

The two places the price card goes quiet

1. Coat and matting are invisible to a size chart

A price card answers "what size is the dog," not "how long will this coat actually take." Both groom the same "medium dog" either way. The calculator prices the coat multiplier and the matting time and surcharge separately, so a curly/doodle coat with moderate matting is visibly a 171-minute job instead of silently the same 69 minutes the card assumes.

2. Add-ons and matting can add up to more than the card charges

This is the one that costs real money. The card charges $75 whether the groom needs three add-ons and a matting surcharge or none at all, but this job's own direct costs — $93 — are already above the $75 the card quotes, before the card fee is even taken out. A groomer working off the card alone can finish a "profitable" day of $75 medium dogs and have actually lost money on the ones that came in matted with add-ons, with nothing on the card to say so in advance.

When the price card is still the better tool

For quoting on the phone, it plainly is. A caller wants one number, not a form, and you usually cannot see the coat before the dog arrives. The sensible arrangement is both: quote the card price to book the appointment, then run this calculator once the dog is on the table to see whether that day's version of "the $75 medium groom" still clears your floor — and, if the coat and matting are bad enough, whether the day-of price needs to move before you start.

Every figure on this page is this calculator's own worked example, not a claim about any real groomer or an industry benchmark. Your rates, coats, and add-on pricing will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Is a flat per-size price card wrong?

No, and it should not go away. A website, a phone quote, or a price list on the wall needs one number per size — "medium dogs $75" is a fine headline price, and no calculator replaces having one. The point of this page is not that the card is wrong. It is that the card is the same number for every medium dog, and a medium poodle with matted fur is not the same job as a medium lab with a smooth coat.

How much do coat type and matting actually add to a groom?

On this calculator's own defaults, a medium-size, medium-coat dog with no matting and no add-ons is a 69-minute groom. Change only the coat to curly/doodle and add moderate matting plus three common add-ons (nail trim, ear cleaning, de-shedding) and the same "medium dog" is a 171-minute groom — nearly three times as long — with $30 of matting surcharge and $52 of add-on charges added on top.

Can the same card price actually lose money?

Yes, and this calculator's own worked example shows exactly that. The simple medium groom nets $61.75 on a $75 card price — an 82.3% margin. The matted, curly-coat, three-add-on medium groom at the identical $75 price has $93 of direct costs before the card fee, so it nets -$20.25 — a real loss, not just a thinner one, because the break-even price for that job ($95.88) is already above the $75 the card charges.

Does the calculator replace the price card?

No, and it is not trying to. The price card is what you quote on the phone before you have seen the coat. This calculator is what you run once the dog is on the table (or from a clear photo and a few questions) to decide whether that day's version of "the $75 medium groom" still clears your floor — and, if the coat and matting are bad enough, whether the card price needs a same-day adjustment before you start.

vs-moego.html.text:
← Pet Grooming Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. MoeGo

Two different shapes: MoeGo is account-based business management software for running a grooming business's whole scheduling-to-payment workflow. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one groom cost, given its size, coat, matting, and add-ons, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

MoeGo is cloud-based business management software built for pet grooming professionals. Its feature set covers 24/7 online booking, appointment scheduling and smart-schedule automation, digital intake forms with e-signatures, a two-way client messaging hub, automated reminders, integrated payment processing, memberships and packages, a client portal, and reporting, with route optimization and map-based scheduling built for mobile groomers specifically. It was founded in late 2019 by Ethan Dong and is headquartered in Culver City, California; it closed a $24 million Series A funding round led by Base10 Partners, with Mars Petcare's Digitalis Ventures also participating, and by 2025 reported serving thousands of pet care businesses across more than 69 million appointments. It is sold as an ongoing monthly subscription, priced per van for mobile groomers or per location for a shop, across tiered plans (reported publicly as roughly $49–$159 per month per van, or $79–$239 per month per location, depending on tier and add-ons such as SMS volume) — this page states no dollar figure as current pricing on MoeGo's own behalf, since plan prices change; see MoeGo's own pricing page for today's numbers.

This calculator does none of what MoeGo does. It does not run a booking calendar, hold a client or appointment record on a server, or process payments. It takes one groom — a dog or cat's size and coat type, matting severity, a checklist of add-ons (nail trim, nail grinding, teeth brushing, ear cleaning, de-shedding, flea/tick treatment, anal gland expression), optional mobile travel time and mileage, hourly wage and payroll burden, supplies, job overhead, payment processing fee, and target margin — and turns that into the contribution left after costs, the break-even quote, the price that hits your target margin, the effective hourly rate, plus a printable customer proposal with scope, deposit split, and a signature line. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. It also does not decide whether an animal is fit or safe to groom — see the calculator's own FAQ on that.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I run a grooming business and need online booking, scheduling, client messaging, and payments handled across every groomer and every appointment.MoeGo, or a comparable grooming-industry platform — running the whole booking-to-payment workflow is not something this calculator does.
Does the price for this one groom actually clear my cost and target margin, once size, coat, matting, and add-ons are counted correctly?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
How much extra should a matted, giant, or curly-coated dog actually cost, once the real time it takes is counted against the job?This calculator's own groom-time and matting-surcharge figures.
I need route optimization and map-based scheduling for a mobile grooming van's whole day.MoeGo — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
How does the math behind a dog grooming price actually work?This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. MoeGo is used through a monthly subscription account, priced per van or per location.

Most groomers get different value from each: MoeGo (or a comparable platform) for running the business's whole booking, client-communication, and payment workflow as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether one job's price actually clears cost and margin before it's quoted — and neither tool makes the welfare or safety call about whether a specific animal should be groomed at all; that stays with the groomer and, where warranted, a veterinarian.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or MoeGo?

They do different jobs. MoeGo is cloud-based business management software built for pet grooming professionals — online booking, scheduling, digital intake forms, two-way client messaging, route optimization for mobile groomers, and integrated payment processing — sold as an ongoing monthly subscription per van or per location. This calculator does none of that. It takes one groom — size, coat, matting severity, add-ons, optional mobile travel, loaded wage, supplies, overhead, and payment fees — and turns that into the contribution after costs, the break-even quote, the price needed to hit a target margin, plus a printable customer proposal, instantly, in the browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A grooming business running scheduling, client communication, and payments across every groomer and every appointment is better served by MoeGo or a comparable platform; a groomer who wants an instant, private, correctly-sized price for one job before it's quoted is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with MoeGo?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by MoeGo. MoeGo is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
